intro: I know you’re going through a lot of applications, so I’ve put together some highlights on how I align with what you’re looking for.

The work I'm proudest of is taking something that grew one piece at a time and making it feel like one system again. That's the problem you're describing! I build and deploy my own sites, so I've been the stressed person staring at a failed deploy, and I'd love to design for that person.

requirements.heading: Making a tangle feel like one obvious thing
requirements.body: At WorkStep, I led a product-wide IA re-architecture with our Senior PM. This project touched navigation, information hierarchy, and dozens of existing features at once. Multi-phase, cross-team, and I owned the direction the whole way through, not just the first few weeks of it.

images.alt: Information architecture work from the WorkStep IA re-architecture

requirements.heading: High-density information design
requirements.body: For four years I designed dashboards, tables, and charts for managers tracking thousands of workers across multiple sites. This involved a lot of hierarchy and prioritization. The Report Builder I created at WorkStep let customers assemble their own views, so effectively a lightweight customizable BI tool that also exported PowerPoint files.

images.alt: Cards from a report builder I designed

requirements.heading: Failure as a first-class state
requirements.body: I write specs that cover the empty, broken, partial, and overloaded states with the same care as the happy path, with numbered callouts so engineers can point at exactly what they're asking about. An error message is an interface, and the person reading it is usually having a bad day. I'd rather design that moment well than hope it doesn't happen.

images.alt: An annotated design spec covering UI states

requirements.heading: Craft that notices the 2px
requirements.body: Typography, spacing, density, and the small feedback that tells you an interaction worked. I set WorkStep's type on a modular scale instead of picking sizes by feel, and I've called out details as small as a subtle scroll shadow in a spec because it changed how the page read. Motion is important to me, too! I've animated in After Effects and Lottie and built hand-drawn frame-by-frame SVG animations for the web.

images.alt: A closeup of a spec I did calling out a specific shadow

requirements.heading: Extending a system instead of fighting it
requirements.body: I rebuilt WorkStep's design system from scratch on Figma variables, tokens, and aliasing, cut component bloat by 85%, and built every color pairing to WCAG AA. I also learned that some things weren't worth standardizing, and established ways to create "starter kits" that avoided people starting from scratch, but allowed flexibility that necessitated prohibitive upkeep and workarounds. Joining Render's system, I'd learn its logic first and then grow it as the surface area grows.

images.alt: Example design system from a project with Halliburton

requirements.heading: Close to the code
requirements.body: I've been writing HTML and CSS since 1999, I maintain my own site in Vue, and I prototype every day with Claude Code. For WorkStep's post-acquisition integration, I prototyped new flows in code so engineers could pressure-test them before anyone committed to a build. This page was published by a workflow I built that turns a job posting into structured data and deploys it to my site.

images.alt: A screenshot of my Claude usage as of recently

requirements.heading: Raising the bar for other designers
requirements.body: At T3 and Foxtrot I mentored designers, ran critiques, helped with hiring, and improved how the team worked. At Unilease I was the first designer and set up the process from nothing. I enjoy helping other designers advance in their careers, challenging them to stay sharp, and learning from them as well. Design critiques are a great avenue for this, but even just banter in Slack and demonstrating a good work ethic goes a long way.

requirements.heading: Where I'd be learning
requirements.body: I haven't designed infrastructure or developer tools as my main product. I've been on the builder side for a long time, writing front-end code since 1999 and deploying my own sites, but service graphs, CI/CD pipelines, and coordinated rollbacks would be new to design for. I'd want to spend real time with Render's users and engineers early, learning where the stress actually lives before redrawing anything.
